summary: Provides guidelines for implementing DNS proxies such as those found in broadband gateways. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Home routers often relay DNS questions for your devices. This tells the makers how to relay without messing up the answers.

questions: how should home gateway dns proxy behave
how should a home gateway dns proxy behave
why do dns proxies break edns0
what is the dns transparency principle
subtitle: How home-router DNS proxies should pass queries along without breaking modern DNS.

tldr.problem: Research found that many broadband gateways contain DNS proxies that are incompatible with current DNS standards, dropping or mangling flags, large responses and extension data.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5625 sets a transparency principle (forward requests and responses verbatim) and adds specific rules on flags, unknown record types, packet size, TCP, EDNS0, TSIG, DHCP defaults and security.
tldr.outcome: It is Best Current Practice 152 and gives implementors a checklist for gateway DNS proxies. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 5625 is Best Current Practice 152, published in August 2009, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Research cited by the RFC ([SAC035] and [DOTSE]) found that many commonly used broadband gateways contain DNS proxies that are incompatible in various ways with current DNS standards. These proxies are usually simple forwarders without caching. They act as a convenient default resolver for clients on the LAN but rely on an upstream resolver, for example at an ISP, to do recursive lookups.

The RFC says it is preferable for client stub resolvers to talk directly to full-feature upstream recursive resolvers wherever possible. Where the client must use the gateway's proxy, the document describes the incompatibilities found and gives implementors guidelines for better interoperability. It uses the RFC 2119 key words.
sections.plainLanguage: Many home routers pass your computer's DNS questions along, and many of them do it badly. This note explains how to do it right.

sections.title: The Transparency Principle
sections.content:
A simple proxy cannot practically implement every current and future DNS feature. The RFC gives reasons: gateways have limited hardware, firmware upgrade cycles are long and many users do not apply upgrades, nobody knows what future DNS features will look like, and supporting them would complicate the configuration interface. Some extensions such as EDNS0 are also meant as hop-by-hop mechanisms, which would force a proxy that counts as a hop to be fully compliant.

Test results in [SAC035] show that the more actively a proxy takes part in the DNS protocol, the more likely it is to interfere with messages. So the proxy's role should be no more and no less than to receive requests from LAN clients, forward them verbatim to a known upstream recursive resolver on the WAN side, and return the whole response verbatim. Proxies are RECOMMENDED to be as transparent as possible.

Except when enforcing an active security or network policy, such as a pre-authentication "walled garden", end-users SHOULD be able to send queries to specified upstream resolvers and bypass the proxy altogether. In that case the gateway SHOULD NOT modify request or response packets in any way.
sections.plainLanguage: A good messenger carries your note exactly as written and brings back the full reply. The less the messenger tinkers, the fewer things go wrong.

sections.title: Flags, Compression and Unknown Record Types
sections.content:
Combined with Postel's Robustness Principle (RFC 793), transparency means a proxy should not arbitrarily reject requests or responses it thinks are non-compliant. Some proxies were seen dropping any packet with the "Authentic Data" (AD) or "Checking Disabled" (CD) bits from DNSSEC. That may stem from RFC 1035 saying the unused "Z" bits MUST be zero, but those bits were always reserved for future use. Proxies MUST ignore unknown DNS flags and proxy the packets as usual.

Label compression (Section 4.1.4 of RFC 1035) is optional, and proxies MUST forward packets whether or not they contain compressed labels. RFC 3597 requires resolvers to handle unknown resource record types transparently, so all requests and responses MUST be proxied regardless of the QTYPE and QCLASS fields, and of the TYPE and CLASS fields of any record inside a response.
sections.plainLanguage: If a letter has a stamp or a sticker the post office has not seen before, it should still deliver the letter, not throw it away.

sections.title: Packet Size, TCP and EDNS0
sections.content:
RFC 1035 limits a DNS payload in a UDP packet to 512 octets. When the required parts of a response do not fit, the server MUST set the "TrunCation" (TC) bit. Many proxies were seen truncating all responses at 512 octets, or at a size tied to the WAN MTU, without setting TC, and others stripping TC from correct server responses. A naive client library could then crash by reading past the data it actually received. Because larger UDP packets are now normal, proxies SHOULD NOT truncate UDP packets over 512 octets. If a proxy must truncate, it MUST set TC, and proxies MUST NOT remove TC from responses.

When a UDP query fails due to truncation, the standard fail-over is to retry over TCP (RFC 1123). Proxies MUST therefore be ready to receive and forward queries over TCP. Some "smart" proxies were seen sending a TCP request upstream over UDP first, which was doomed to be truncated. A proxy that receives a request over TCP SHOULD forward it over TCP and SHOULD NOT try UDP first.

EDNS0 (RFC 2671) lets a client put an OPT record in the Additional Section to advertise a receive buffer size and the "DNSSEC OK" (DO) flag. Some proxies rejected such packets with a FORMERR response code or silently discarded them. Proxies MUST NOT refuse to proxy them.

Large UDP packets can exceed the WAN MTU, and gateways handle fragments in one of three ways: drop them, forward them individually, or reassemble and re-fragment. Dropping fragments breaks EDNS0 unless the client advertises a buffer size limited to the WAN MTU less the IP header size. EDNS0 allows buffers up to 65535 octets, but most common servers do not support above 4096, so proxies SHOULD forward UDP packets with payloads of at least 4096 octets whichever method they use.
sections.plainLanguage: Short messages fit on a postcard. Long ones need a bigger envelope. If the postcard is cut short, the messenger must say so, and must be able to carry the big envelope too.

sections.title: TSIG Signed Messages
sections.content:
TSIG (RFC 2845) authenticates DNS requests and responses at the packet level. Any change to the DNS portions of a signed packet, other than the Query ID, causes an authentication failure.

Proxies MUST implement Section 4.7 of RFC 2845 and either forward packets unchanged or fully implement TSIG. They MUST also be able to proxy packets containing TKEY (RFC 2930) records. The RFC adds that a proxy which transparently intercepts all DNS queries and returns unsigned answers to signed queries, as commonly found in WiFi hotspot walled gardens, will also cause TSIG failures.
sections.plainLanguage: A signed letter has a wax seal. If the messenger changes the words, the seal breaks, so the messenger must leave signed letters alone.

sections.title: How DHCP Points Clients at the Proxy
sections.content:
Most consumers get their network settings from DHCP (RFC 2131), including DNS settings. Most gateways default to supplying their own address in the "Domain Name Server" option (Option 6, RFC 2132), so clients use the proxy unless reconfigured. Some gateways use the ISP-supplied DNS values only for their own forwarding and do not offer them over DHCP, leaving hard-coding in the client as the only escape, which is poor for mobile devices. Gateways are therefore RECOMMENDED to let the device administrator configure the Option 6 values.

For the "Domain Name" option (Option 15), the RFC notes that a significant amount of traffic to the DNS Root Name Servers is for invalid top-level domain names, some traceable to vendor firmware defaults. Since there is no standard for a local suffix, the default SHOULD be empty and the option MUST NOT be sent when no value is configured.

Lease timing matters too. A lease obtained while the WAN link is down will carry the gateway's own address until renewed. The RFC offers no firm rule, but suggests considering lease length, forcing a renewal, persisting learned upstream values (at the risk of stale values if the device moves to another ISP), or issuing only 60 second leases while the WAN is down. With that last approach the RFC says a DNS proxy might not be needed at all.
sections.plainLanguage: When your device joins the network, the router tells it who to ask for directions. The router should let its owner change that answer and should not hand out made-up names.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document introduces no new protocols but lists vendor recommendations. On forgery resilience, many proxies pick a new Query ID for outbound requests so answers go to the right client; that is acceptable even with TSIG, because the signature uses the original message ID carried in the TSIG record. However, many proxies were seen using sequential Query IDs. Proxies are strongly RECOMMENDED to follow RFC 5452, particularly Section 9.2 on randomising Query IDs and source ports, including source ports in any NAT function. A proxy on a gateway with NAT compliant with RFC 4787 SHOULD also follow Section 10 of RFC 5452 on how long DNS state is kept.

Some gateways listen on both LAN and WAN interfaces, which allows reflector attacks as described in RFC 5358. The proxy SHOULD NOT, by default, be reachable from the WAN.

Deep packet inspection sits uneasily with transparency, but the RFC separates malformed traffic from merely unexpected data. Packets that MAY be dropped include those with invalid compression pointers (outside the packet or causing a parsing loop) and incorrect Question, Answer, Authority or Additional counts, with care where truncation is possible. Silent drops make clients retransmit and notice the error late, so proxies SHOULD synthesise an error response such as SERVFAIL instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The messenger should not use easy-to-guess ticket numbers, should only serve people inside the house, and should say "something is wrong" rather than staying silent.

viz.caption: PROXY MISBEHAVIOUR AND WHAT THE RFC REQUIRES

SHOULD NOT truncate; if it must, MUST set TC
Removing the TC bit from server responses
No TCP support, or retrying a TCP request over UDP first
MUST forward over TCP; SHOULD NOT try UDP first
Rejecting or black-holing packets with an OPT record
MUST NOT refuse to proxy them
SHOULD forward UDP payloads of at least 4096 octets
